title: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms
author: Emelie Skoghag

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Skoghag materially develops the cluster’s lawyer–engineer collaboration proposition by explaining why legal technologists must translate lawyers’ high-level accounts into explicit workflow steps, communications and deliverables. The source does not address human verification or the copilot-versus-autopilot question.
qs: So it's quite easy to describe a general workflow, but then when you do try to specify it, it usually tends to narrow down to well, it depends.
What needs to be a part of the deliverable here?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Skoghag strongly accepts the cluster’s process-led redesign proposition and materially develops it with practical guidance: identify the problem and map workflows before procurement, design around heterogeneous client data, assess value using process-specific and experience-based measures, and use firmwide mapping to identify shared workflows and testing opportunities. Her forecast that AI will shift junior tasks rather than eliminate junior lawyers also aligns with the cluster’s cautious labour-market framing, though it is predictive rather than empirical.
qs: I think you have to start off with the groundwork and actually do the process mapping and see what can be improved with sort of the quick wins today before moving on to actually  finding a tool that's suiting the issue.
I think we're going to see a shift in what type of tasks a junior might have done in the past comparatively to what they do today.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s workflow-design proposition by advocating iterative, problem-first implementation rather than imposing AI on inherited processes. Its account of non-lawyer developers productively challenging legal routines also supports workflow redesign, though it does not substantively address client context, expert testing, tacit knowledge transfer or human verification.
qs: So for example, how to build an AI enabled workflow, but rather you start off with the core issue.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that automating traditional junior tasks disrupts legal training and makes deliberate mentorship more important. It is more optimistic about juniors moving into higher-value work and does not develop the cluster’s verification paradox or concrete simulation-based response; its claims are predictions rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Um but I see a shift in the role of mentorship and I think that mentorship will take a much larger role that it will be less of sort of the filling out forms work that may have been tasks of the past where we can  automate a large chunk today with the use of AI and other tools.

I do think there's going to be a awkward few years perhaps where we we need to iron out the kinks of how training actually is going to be done and how do you tackle those questions and I I don't think that's something that I will be able to answer today.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that automating routine junior work creates an unresolved apprenticeship problem requiring greater mentorship and redesigned training. st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that automation will remove routine junior work and disrupt traditional training, making mentorship more important. It also predicts that juniors will move toward higher-value strategic responsibilities, while acknowledging that the transition and training model remain unresolved.
qs: Um but I see a shift in the role of mentorship and I think that mentorship will take a much larger role that it will be less of sort of the filling out forms work that may have been tasks of the past where we can  automate a large chunk today with the use of AI and other tools.

So I think a lot of that will go and you end up doing the sort of work that I wanted to do as a junior lawyer, you know, the higher value stuff like thinking about strategy and advising on the case on how to develop the arguments and and interviewing witnesses and doing negotiations and settling cases, stuff like that.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: Skoghag supports the cluster’s selective data-preparation approach: firms should make internal records coherent and reliable while designing procurement and workflows to tolerate client inputs that cannot conform to uniform metadata standards. The source is experience-based and does not demonstrate measured outcomes.
qs: How do we structure our own documents and how do we structure our own you know management systems and throughout how do we make that neat coherent and reliable?

it frankly not realistic that we can require the exact same level of structure works as what we currently have in our mapping systems with metadata etc etc so I think you do need to be mindful when you're both in  procurement and in building workflows later on that you need to have structures in place to allow for that flexibility.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s organisational-redesign proposition by arguing that legal delivery processes should be mapped and improved before technology is selected. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that transformation is not achieved merely by purchasing software, while treating changes to junior work as task redesign rather than established wholesale displacement.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central view that AI will reorganise legal production and junior task composition rather than eliminate lawyers. It expects routine work to be automated and juniors redirected toward higher-value activity and mentorship, while acknowledging unresolved training and implementation challenges.
qs: I don't think it's going to be as apocalyptic as some of the legal news reported to be.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Skoghag supports the cluster’s view that resistance is not adequately explained by lawyers being inherently conservative. She reports substantial openness to innovation despite heavy workloads, while making successful receptiveness conditional on proper organisational preparation. The source offers experiential observations rather than measured implementation outcomes.
qs: So, something that surprised me the  most, I would say, is that people often tend to underestimate how open-minded lawyers are to change.
So, I would actually say that with the right preparations, it's not a hurdle.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Skoghag supports the proposition that legal AI will reshape junior lawyers’ task mix without necessarily eliminating junior roles. Her optimism about AI-native entrants is a forecast about adaptation, not evidence that existing staffing levels or business models will be preserved.

kp.k: Legal technologists integrate procurement, implementation and business improvement
kp.d: Skoghag describes her role as spanning tool selection, firmwide implementation, upskilling, workflow building and innovation. Rather than acquiring technology speculatively, she starts with colleagues' or clients' frustrations and connects tools across the existing technology stack to avoid unused licences. The host frames this intersection of law and technology as an emerging profession.
qs: being a legal technologist pertains to working in the intersection between tech and law.

it's a long process of primarily focusing on the frustrations and pain points of the colleagues or clients that we are working with all the way up to adoption, implementation, upskilling and then building workflows within those tools.
obviously you don't want to use those tools in a silo.

kp.k: Legal knowledge helps uncover tacit workflow requirements
kp.d: Skoghag says legal training helps technologists elicit granular requirements when lawyers struggle to explain their processes beyond generalities or 'it depends', but is not essential. Separately, the host reports that non-lawyer developers sometimes challenge inherited practices and propose more rational alternatives.
qs: I think having a legal background can definitely aid in that but it's not a requirement I would say by any means but the factf finding mission sure is easier.
So they might say, well then I contact the client, but how do you do it? Is it an email? What's in the email? What's in the contents? What needs to be a part of the deliverable here?

kp.k: Diagnose problems and redesign processes before buying technology
kp.d: Skoghag recommends an iterative sequence of identifying the underlying frustration, mapping the process and only then considering a product. Some improvements require no technology; attempting to fit a tool to every inherited process detail can make implementation excessively complicated. She consequently advocates openness to adapting processes to tools.
qs: there might be changes to the process that could be implemented today that doesn't require any tech at all where it's just a unspoken rule or norm where it's always being done that way and no one's ever challenged why that is.
you might have to be open to adjust the process to fit the tool rather than the the opposite.

kp.k: Firmwide mapping reveals similarities across practice groups
kp.d: Drawing on her experience, Skoghag reports that offering partners one-hour sessions on the existing technology stack also elicited descriptions of their daily work. Comparing document types, material volumes and work scope revealed similarities across legal fields and helped identify relevant practice groups for subsequent tool testing. This is a practitioner account, not a quantified assessment of resulting efficiencies.
qs: I offered sort of a one-to-one partner session with all the partners at the firm where you could book an hour with me where I would go through the current legal tech stack that we had with a goal of keeping everyone up to speed.
It doesn't really have to do with tech at all, but it did help us to identify the core practice groups when testing certain types of tools.

kp.k: Workflow design requires multiple perspectives and human checkpoints
kp.d: Skoghag distinguishes large end-to-end legal process projects, requiring workshops and potentially multiple practice groups, from individual task workflows that can be investigated through interviews. Mapping should establish current practice, expectations, metrics, formalities and where humans remain involved. Independently consulting other lawyers helps distinguish core requirements from individual habits; her references to control groups concern process elicitation, not experimental AI testing.
qs: if you talk about the workflow that's end to end legal process that's quite a large project. It usually involves tons of lawyers and a real workshop setup.
where you need humans in the loop

you do kind of need to have a few reference points, control groups where you're checking up and asking people independently of each other to make sure that you're not following the whim of someone who's done it that way since eternity

kp.k: Customisation can support adoption and clarify junior expectations
kp.d: Skoghag recommends accommodating strongly held working preferences where feasible, for example through flexible milestones, partner-specific writing examples or specified final checks. She argues that contemporary AI can support bespoke workflows using a few good examples rather than the large training and validation datasets associated with earlier machine-learning tools. Making partner expectations explicit can also reduce uncertainty for juniors.
qs: If it's very clear that certain individuals have a strong preference in their ways of working, you can actually shift your mindset to see that as a feature rather than an issue.
Whereas today you could probably make use of a few good examples.
you're codifying those uncertainties that I'm sure that a lot of junior lawyers have regardless.

kp.k: Engaging formats and gamification may improve technology adoption
kp.d: Skoghag advocates creative learning formats and game elements to address busy lawyers' information fatigue and resistance to learning. Examples include leaderboards, recognition and staged checklists in tool pilots. She reports that colleagues still asked about a rapid-question office-tour video nearly 3 years later, offering anecdotal evidence of memorable communication rather than measured adoption gains.
qs: being able to deliver any sort of content in a engaging enthusiastic manner is definitely a way to combat sort of the information fatigue or the resistance to learning
it's integrating game elements uh like points, tier lists, challenges, games to sort of raise motivation or raise engagement.
it's something that I still get asked about nearly 3 years later if I still have that video.

kp.k: Impact measurement should include experience, not just usage
kp.d: Skoghag argues that metrics should reflect each process's intended value, distinguishing cost reduction from quality or trust. She describes difficulty connecting raw usage statistics to actual benefits and proposes return on experience alongside return on investment. Interviews and questionnaires should complement usage data to capture client and colleague experience, satisfaction, retention and quality; no numerical impact estimates are supplied.
qs: I think it's dependent on what you pick as a value metric to be honest.
not just return on investment rather return on experience.
conducting in-depth interviews or sending out questionnaires based on experience etc etc to sort of complement the picture and to get the full gist of the actual added benefit.

kp.k: Legal AI must accommodate unstructured external data
kp.d: Skoghag distinguishes maintaining coherent internal documents and systems from dealing with clients whose data cannot realistically be required to follow identical structures. She recommends incorporating input flexibility into procurement and workflow design, pressing suppliers to support practical ingestion options, and establishing processes to structure incoming material, potentially using AI. She cautions that unforeseen data problems will continue to arise.
qs: we cannot enforce our clients to use the same neat structured boxes that uh that we use.
It's really hard to build a workflow based on everything working as it's supposed to.

it's the balance of keeping the own data structured, having the flexibility of taking in raw data that is completely unstructured and implementing implementing good systems and processes on our side on how to structure that raw unstructured data.

kp.d: The host reports that Garfield must handle both programmatic court API exchanges and unstructured emails from court officials whose processes differ. He predicts that expanded APIs and eventual common standards, including standards imposed through court systems, will improve data consistency. These are the host's operational observations and expectations, not Skoghag's findings.
qs: some parts of the process are handled by the API but then there's some parts of it that suddenly you start getting emails from court officials
you then have to end up building a tool that can handle multiple different forms of data.
as courts start to deploy APIs that will inevitably impose standards upon people that use the court services

kp.k: Junior work may shift toward mentorship and higher-value tasks
kp.d: Skoghag predicts a change in junior task composition rather than the apocalyptic outcome she attributes to some legal news coverage. She anticipates greater reliance on mentorship and an awkward transition lasting perhaps a few years while training is redesigned, explicitly declining to offer a settled solution. Separately, the host predicts that automating due diligence, disclosure and note-taking will allow juniors to do more strategy, argument development, witness interviewing and negotiation.
qs: I think we're going to see a shift in what type of tasks a junior might have done in the past comparatively to what they do today.
I do think there's going to be a awkward few years perhaps where we we need to iron out the kinks of how training actually is going to be done
I see a shift in the role of mentorship and I think that mentorship will take a much larger role

kp.k: AI sounding boards offer anecdotal support for junior confidence
kp.d: The host recounts an unnamed junior's claim that a legal technology 'buddy' reduced stress by answering questions she felt uncomfortable asking busy colleagues; she believed she could assess whether its answers were sensible. Skoghag reports a similar statement from one junior associate in a post-pilot interview, tentatively dated February of 2024, about using AI to test ideas and regain confidence. These are individual reported experiences, not evidence of a general reduction in lawyers' stress or validated answer accuracy.
qs: most of the time she feels like she's got the level experience already to be able to evaluate whether the answer is a sensible one or not.
Gosh, it must have been in February of 2024 or something
one of the junior associates specifically said the added benefit of having a legal buddy that she could use as sounding board.
other times it might just have been sufficient to use it as a sounding board get a quick recall and then be confident again and moving on.

kp.k: Prepared innovation initiatives can encounter receptive lawyers
kp.d: Skoghag says her experience contradicted her expectation that lawyers would be too busy to engage with process improvement. She attributes increasing openness, particularly since the AI boom, partly to perceptions that tools can now be implemented quickly. Her description of growth is qualitative and conditional on appropriate preparation, rather than a measured adoption trend.
qs: people often tend to underestimate how open-minded lawyers are to change.
with the right preparations, it's not a hurdle.
whereas today people can see that we can be up and running in quite little time.
I definitely had a a preconceived notion that people were going to be too busy to talk. I've found the opposite to be true completely.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Skoghag describes legal technologists as integrating procurement, process improvement, implementation and AI-enabled workflow building across a law firm.
pts.d: Drawing on her own role at DLA Piper Sweden, Skoghag describes an end-to-end function that starts with colleagues' or clients' problems and extends through adoption, upskilling and connecting tools within the firm's technology stack. She says a legal background helps uncover the details of legal processes but is not a requirement. She does not herself claim that AI created this profession.

pts.k: Skoghag argues that successful AI-enabled workflows require diagnosing problems and redesigning processes, rather than simply fitting technology to existing practices.
pts.d: Her approach separates the underlying issue, process mapping and product selection. She says some improvements require no technology, while forcing a tool to fit an unchanged, complicated process may leave no suitable product. Firmwide mapping also reveals similarities between practice groups and helps identify appropriate groups for tool testing.

pts.k: Skoghag says current AI makes bespoke workflows easier to build, including accommodation of individual partners' preferences.
pts.d: She contrasts current AI's ability to use a few examples with earlier machine-learning approaches requiring substantial training and validation data. Her examples include separate sets of firm precedents reflecting different partners' writing styles and flexible workflow milestones. She argues that identifying these preferences can improve adoption and make previously implicit expectations explicit for junior lawyers. This is a practical account of customization, not a quantified model-performance claim.

pts.k: Skoghag claims that engaging communication and gamification can reduce information fatigue and support legal-technology adoption.
pts.d: She describes points, challenges, recognition, leaderboards and staged checklists as ways to increase motivation or engagement. Examples from her firm include gamified pilot checklists and a rapid-question office-tour video about legal technology. The video provides an anecdote about lasting engagement rather than a measured increase in AI use.

pts.k: Skoghag argues that the value of AI and new workflows includes user experience and quality, and cannot be inferred from usage statistics alone.
pts.d: She proposes examining return on experience alongside return on investment, linking colleagues' and clients' experiences to satisfaction, retention and quality. This is a recommendation for assessing impact, not evidence that particular tools have increased retention or reduced costs. She says metrics should depend on whether the objective is cost reduction, quality enhancement or trust, with interviews and questionnaires supplementing raw usage data.

pts.k: Skoghag says AI can help structure incoming unstructured data, but legal workflows must remain flexible because firms cannot impose their internal data standards on clients.
pts.d: She describes the operational requirement as balancing structured internal documents and systems with the ability to receive inconsistent external material. Procurement and workflow design should anticipate varied inputs, and firms should press suppliers for flexible ingestion features. She does not predict that data variability will disappear.

pts.k: Skoghag predicts a change in junior lawyers' tasks and a larger role for mentorship, rather than an apocalyptic outcome for junior lawyers.
pts.d: She expects AI and other tools to automate a substantial portion of form-filling work and change juniors' task mix. She suggests younger entrants' existing familiarity with AI will make workplace use seem normal. However, she anticipates a difficult transition in training and explicitly does not offer a settled solution. She gives no prediction about junior headcount, hiring rates or staffing leverage.

pts.k: Skoghag reports that a junior associate found an AI legal 'buddy' useful as a sounding board and a source of renewed confidence.
pts.d: Skoghag confirms that she encountered feedback matching the discussion of junior-lawyer reassurance in an in-depth post-pilot interview. Her concrete evidence is one associate's reported experience, not a measured firmwide reduction in stress. The use described is augmentation through questions and idea development, not autonomous legal work or demonstrated accuracy of the tool's answers.

pts.k: Skoghag says lawyers are more receptive to innovation than commonly assumed, and that openness has increased since the AI boom.
pts.d: She reports that, with appropriate preparation, lawyers actively seek improvements and make time for them despite heavy workloads. She connects increased openness with the perception that tools can now be deployed relatively quickly. Her description of growth as exponential is an experiential characterization; no adoption series or implementation-time data are supplied.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies principally on Skoghag's implementation experience, concrete internal examples and qualitative feedback; its future-of-work claims are predictions.
pts.d: Her evidence includes firmwide process mapping, individual partner sessions, workflow customization, pilot checklists, an engaging internal video and a post-pilot junior-associate interview. The partner sessions reportedly helped reveal cross-practice similarities and select testing groups. The video reportedly remained memorable nearly three years later. No quantitative productivity, accuracy, cost, retention, stress or employment results are presented, and no external study or model benchmark is cited. Her predictions about junior tasks and mentorship are explicitly framed as her expectations.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current implementation claims are distinguished from near-future predictions, with training uncertainty and organizational preparation as important qualifications.
pts.d: In the document identified as a 2026 episode, Skoghag presents customization with a few examples, partial automation and faster tool setup as present capabilities. She places the junior-role transition in the near future, anticipates an 'awkward few years' and describes training as an ongoing discussion without a fixed endpoint. She approximately dates the associate interview to February 2024. Successful implementation is conditional on problem diagnosis, process mapping, appropriate human involvement, accommodation of preferences, flexible data handling and preparation for adoption. She supplies no dated forecast for market-wide transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern law-firm personnel and their clients, particularly legal technologists, partners and junior associates.
pts.d: Legal technologists coordinate cross-practice improvement, procurement, training and connected workflows. Partners contribute process knowledge and preferences that can be incorporated into tool-supported work. Junior lawyers face a changing task mix, less ambiguity about partner expectations, potentially useful AI sounding boards and unresolved training needs. Colleagues and clients are the proposed beneficiaries whose experience, quality and satisfaction should inform value assessment. Technology suppliers are expected to accommodate inconsistent client data. The source does not offer concrete claims about ALSP market share, in-house displacement, public access to justice or firm staffing reductions.
